extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of mythology, folklore, and comparative religion
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and methodological criteria for analysing myths, distinguishing myth from history, and studying the relation between ritual, tradition, and myth in folkloristics and comparative religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of recurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the tale bear a strong resemblance in more than one of its circumstances to any other tradition or group of traditions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recurrence to judge whether a tale is mythic or historical; the student must be constantly on guard. The test of recurrence is helpful but not always sufficient because myth may group with folklore and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradition as primary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The tradition itself affords the chief if not the only sure evidence of its age, its origin, and its meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the content and form of oral tradition when evaluating age/origin/meaning; do not rely solely on the date or nature of the earliest written text. Investigate preservation influences before assigning authority to a recorded form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date and circumstances of literary reduction as important but not decisive
rubrics_metrics.description: The date when and the circumstances in which a tradition is first reduced to literary form are important factors in the evidence as to the credibility of the particular form in which the tradition is preserved; but they are not all the factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the first literary attestation as one factor among many — examine the wider oral history, modes of preservation, and context rather than assuming greater antiquity simply because a text is older.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume ritual can generate myth (method for rudimentary religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sound method in dealing with myth as associated with ritual at the stage of rudimentary religion to assume that for the most part it is the ritual that generates the myth, and not the myth the ritual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with late-origin explanatory myths attached to ritual, consider that such myths are likely post hoc and relatively late; but treat this assumption as methodological (not absolute) and test against other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equating myth with history
rubrics_metrics.description: Because mythic tradition has been found to include many traditions which of late years have been claimed to belong to a definitely historical race of people, it must not be identified with history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware both the disastrous appropriation of tradition wholly to mythology and the equally disastrous rejection of tradition and the historical event round which it clusters; separate mythic elements from verifiable historical fact carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search diligently for metamorphoses between fact, myth, and history
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition from fact or surmise to myth, myth to pseudo-history, or from history to myth, and then perhaps to history again; from legend to history, from history to legend, or from folk-tale to history—these metamorphoses must be searched for diligently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace the trajectories by which narratives change classification over time; look for points where oral transmission, literary fixation, or ritual attachment produced shifts in status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparative method and Tylor's test
rubrics_metrics.description: Tylor laid stress upon the value of the comparison of myth and the 'test of recurrence.' He did not entirely discount philological evidence, but denied the large place claimed for allegory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply systematic comparison across traditions to detect patterns and laws of formation; be cautious about allegorical interpretations and emphasize recurrence and comparative patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tylor's animistic hypothesis (landmark)
rubrics_metrics.description: The promulgation of the animistic hypothesis by Tylor is a landmark in mythic science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider animism (the attribution of spirits/agency to natural phenomena) as a foundational explanatory framework for many myths; use it as one theoretical lens rather than a universal answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lang's methodological contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Lang demonstrated the unsoundness of the 'disease of language' theory; he laid stress on the irrational element in myth; indicated the complexity of mythic development; showed how the evolutionary theory may be applied to myth; pointed out that the persistence of myth was accounted for by religious conservatism; and laid it down that the occurrence of identical myths may be accounted for by the universal prevalence of similar mental habits (though this will not account for long and intricate plots).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluation, allow for multiple causal factors (irrational elements, evolution, conservatism, universal mental habits); avoid single-factor explanations for complex parallels and long narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection of myth by ritual
rubrics_metrics.description: Jevons points out the reflection of myth by ritual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying ritual, look for how ritual practice preserves, mirrors, or reshapes mythic narratives; use ritual evidence as a complementary source for reconstructing mythic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's methodological stance (three propositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) That myth is for the most part sacred in character; (ii) That it is prior in origin to ritual and is not derived from it, except in a secondary sense; (iii) That mythic conditions are capable of a more or less exact classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the author's working hypotheses to guide classification and interpretation: treat myth as often sacred, consider myth before ritual in origin unless evidence indicates otherwise, and attempt systematic classification of mythic types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative philology for names and origins
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand the origin and meaning of the names of the Greek gods and to enter into the original intention of the fables told of each, we must take into account the collateral evidence supplied by Latin, German, Sanskrit, and Zend philology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inquiries into etymology and name-meanings should deploy evidence across related languages to illuminate original meanings and possible loan-words or semantic shifts.
